clue.text: Literate punters found in lecturer's joint

parts.note: a reader is a senior university lecturer in Britain, here with the possessive S
the hip is a joint of the body

explanation.surface: Bookish gamblers turn up at a don's favourite haunt.
explanation.walkthrough: In British universities a READER ranks just below a professor; 'joint' looks like a pub or dive but is the body's HIP.
explanation.definitionFit: A publication's readers collectively are its audience of literate customers, the people who buy and read it.

clue.text: A rate arranged for lasso

indicators.note: arranged tells us the letters of a and rate are set out in a new order

explanation.surface: A fee is fixed for hiring a lasso.
explanation.definitionFit: A reata is a rope with a running noose used by cowboys, the same thing as a lariat.

clue.text: Marathon participant outlasted many in dramatic competition

explanation.surface: A runner in the long race kept going longer than the other actors.
explanation.walkthrough: Not a runner: the Athenian tragedian fought against the Persians at the battle of Marathon and won many prizes at the Dionysia drama contests.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek tragic poet fought at the battle of Marathon in 490 BC and won the Athenian drama festival repeatedly.

clue.text: Possibly be a folk emperor under King John

indicators.note: possibly says the letters of be a folk emperor may be read in some other arrangement

explanation.surface: A common ruler might serve beneath a medieval English monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: William Marshal, the great earl who served King John, also appears as a character in Shakespeare's play King John.
explanation.definitionFit: The title was held by William Marshal, a magnate and loyal servant of the monarch, and he figures in Shakespeare's history play.

clue.text: Working hard starting some literary and very intellectual new gathering

indicators.note: starting points to the opening letter of each of the following seven words

parts.words: some literary and very intellectual new gathering

explanation.surface: Some bookish and brainy folk toil at founding a fresh salon.
explanation.definitionFit: To slave is to toil like a drudge, so labouring strenuously is this.

clue.text: "Volumes might be written upon the - - of the pious" (Herbert Spencer)

definitions.text: "Volumes might be written upon the - - of the pious" (Herbert Spencer)

parts.words: "Volumes might be written upon the - - of the pious" (Herbert Spencer)
parts.note: a quotation from the philosopher Spencer with one word missing; the gap wants the opposite of the godliness of the pious

explanation.surface: A line from Herbert Spencer with a word left out for the solver to supply.
explanation.walkthrough: A literary fill-in: the missing word makes Spencer's ironic point that the devout can be irreverent.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap is filled by a word for irreverence or lack of piety, which is what Spencer paradoxically charged the pious with.

clue.text: Potted biography mostly found in book of the Apocrypha

indicators.note: mostly means the book's name loses one letter, keeping most of it

parts.note: Tobit is a book of the Apocrypha telling of the pious Tobit and his son Tobias

explanation.surface: A short life story turns up in one of the books outside the canon.
explanation.definitionFit: A death notice in a newspaper summarises a person's life, a potted life story.

clue.text: He wanted his heart buried at Wounded Knee

definitions.text: He wanted his heart buried at Wounded Knee

parts.words: He wanted his heart buried at Wounded Knee
parts.note: points to the American poet whose poem American Names ends with a wish to have his heart laid at that South Dakota site

explanation.surface: A man's last wish about where his heart should rest.
explanation.walkthrough: Stephen Vincent Benét's poem 'American Names' closes 'Bury my heart at Wounded Knee'.
explanation.definitionFit: The American poet Stephen Vincent wrote the line in his poem American Names, so the clue identifies him by it.

clue.text: The tigers of wrath are wiser than - - of instruction" (Blake)

explanation.surface: A Blake proverb with two words left for the solver to supply.
explanation.walkthrough: From Blake's Proverbs of Hell in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap holds the trained steeds Blake contrasts with wild tigers, schooled beasts of the stable.

clue.text: A brace of seamen, perhaps, from Dickens

explanation.surface: Two sailors, say, as described by a Victorian novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: A brace is a pair and sailors are 'hands'; the phrase is also the title of a piece by Dickens.
explanation.definitionFit: Two deckhands make a couple of crew members, and the phrase is also a title from the Victorian novelist's writings.

clue.text: Whence the love-light of Spain rode to the sea

definitions.text: Whence the love-light of Spain rode to the sea

parts.words: Whence the love-light of Spain rode to the sea
parts.note: recalls Chesterton's Lepanto, where Don John, love-light of Spain, is riding to the sea; the clue asks for the country in his title

explanation.surface: A poetic question about where a Spanish hero set out from.
explanation.walkthrough: G.K. Chesterton's 'Lepanto': 'Love-light of Spain - hurrah! ... Don John of Austria is riding to the sea.'
explanation.definitionFit: Don John of the poem takes his name from the Habsburg land, so that country is where the hero comes from.

clue.text: The man hath — done,/And — more will do." (Coleridge)

definitions.text: The man hath — done,/And — more will do." (Coleridge)

parts.words: The man hath — done,/And — more will do." (Coleridge)

explanation.surface: Two lines of Coleridge with the same word left out twice.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken of the Mariner in Part V of 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner'.
explanation.definitionFit: The gaps want the atonement for sin the Mariner performs for shooting the albatross.

clue.text: Moore protagonist badly atrophied

indicators.note: badly signals the letters of atrophied are put into a disordered new arrangement

explanation.surface: A novelist's heroine has wasted away dreadfully.
explanation.walkthrough: George Moore wrote 'Aphrodite in Aulis' (1930).
explanation.definitionFit: George Moore's late novel Aphrodite in Aulis takes the Greek love goddess as its title figure.

clue.text: Amoretto is supplied

explanation.surface: A little cupid has been provided.
explanation.walkthrough: An amoretto is a cherub in art; 'put to' can mean supplied or set before someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name a winged cherub figure in Renaissance art, and the phrase split in two means provided or offered.

clue.text: Housman's "land of lost content"

parts.note: A Shropshire Lad calls the poet's remembered county the land of lost content; the clue wants that county's old name

explanation.surface: The poet's phrase for a vanished, happy homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: In 'A Shropshire Lad' XL Housman calls it 'the land of lost content'; SALOP is an old name for Shropshire, an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: Housman's poem looks back on the English county of his Lad, whose traditional abbreviated name is this.

clue.text: Eponymous tram not featured in play

definitions.text: Eponymous tram not featured in play

parts.words: Eponymous tram not featured in play
parts.note: Tennessee Williams named his play after a New Orleans tram called Desire that never appears on stage

explanation.surface: A tram gives its name to a drama but never appears in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A Streetcar Named Desire' takes its title from the tram line, which is never seen.
explanation.definitionFit: A tram is an American trolley, the vehicle in Williams's title A Named Desire.

clue.text: Chap flowers in Simms book

parts.note: a guy is a chap or fellow
a flower is a thing that flows, a crossword name for a river

explanation.surface: A man's blooms appear in a novel by an American author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flowers' are things that flow, i.e. rivers. William Gilmore Simms wrote the novel 'Guy Rivers' (1834).
explanation.definitionFit: Guy Rivers is a frontier romance by William Gilmore Simms, the South Carolina novelist.

clue.text: Immerse it, curiously, in the calling of Peter, Tasso's holy author of the crusade

definitions.text: the calling of Peter, Tasso's holy author of the crusade

indicators.note: curiously indicates the letters of immerse it are found in an odd new arrangement

explanation.surface: Plunging in oddly forms the vocation of a holy man from an Italian epic.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter the Hermit, who preached the First Crusade, appears in Tasso's 'Jerusalem Delivered'.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter the Hermit's vocation was the solitary religious life, the life of a recluse.

clue.text: Had he not-/ My father as he slept" (Hamlet)

definitions.text: Had he not-/ My father as he slept" (Hamlet)

parts.words: Had he not-/ My father as he slept" (Hamlet)
parts.note: a Shakespeare line with one word missing; the sleeping king looked like the speaker's father, so the gap wants looked like

explanation.surface: A line of Shakespeare with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is actually Lady Macbeth's in Macbeth II.ii ('Had he not resembled / My father as he slept, I had done't'), though the clue credits Hamlet.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap needs a verb meaning looked like, as the sleeping King Duncan looked like Lady Macbeth's own father.

clue.text: How dead conducted Roman church

parts.note: late means dead, as in the late king

explanation.surface: A question about how the dead were led in a Roman basilica.
explanation.walkthrough: St John Lateran is the cathedral church of Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: St John Lateran is the cathedral of the Bishop of Rome, the Pope's own basilica.

clue.text: Active -like Frank Capra's best-loved hero?

explanation.surface: A busy man resembles the hero of a Capra film.
explanation.walkthrough: Capra's 'Mr Deeds Goes to Town' gives the playful second sense: full of Deeds.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic adjective means full of action, and playfully suggests a likeness to Capra's Mr Deeds.

clue.text: Scenarist somehow dotes on the stage

indicators.note: somehow says the letters of dotes are put together in an unspecified fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A screenwriter is besotted with the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: Clifford Odets wrote plays and Hollywood screenplays.
explanation.definitionFit: Clifford Odets was an American playwright who also wrote film screenplays.

clue.text: As poor Tom, he was a cold

definitions.text: As poor Tom, he was a cold

parts.words: As poor Tom, he was a cold

explanation.surface: Poor Tom was chilly.
explanation.walkthrough: In King Lear the disguised son of Gloucester cries 'Poor Tom's a-cold'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloucester's legitimate son in King Lear disguises himself as the beggar Poor Tom.

clue.text: Fraternal, but dour, we hear, teller of tales

indicators.note: we hear says the word for dour is spoken and a like-sounding spelling taken

explanation.surface: A brotherly but stern storyteller, so it is said.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fraternal' points to the Brothers Grimm, the German collectors of folk tales.
explanation.definitionFit: Jacob and Wilhelm, the German brothers, collected and published folk stories.

clue.text: Seats for lonesco piece

explanation.surface: Furniture for a play by an absurdist dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: Eugène Ionesco's absurdist play 'Les Chaises' is known in English by this title.
explanation.definitionFit: Seats are pieces of furniture to sit on, and Ionesco's absurdist one-act play has that English title.

clue.text: Mensa gang harbours French novelist

indicators.note: harbours says the answer is held inside the run of letters in Mensa gang

explanation.surface: A clever society's group shelters a writer from France.
explanation.definitionFit: Françoise Sagan wrote Bonjour Tristesse and other novels in France.

clue.text: Smollett's slag

explanation.surface: A novelist's waste from the furnace.
explanation.walkthrough: Smollett's last novel is 'The Expedition of Humphry Clinker'.
explanation.definitionFit: Humphry is the title hero of Smollett's novel, and the word also means fused residue left in a furnace.

clue.text: The discovery of Nina Bawden

explanation.surface: Something the novelist Nina Bawden came across.
explanation.walkthrough: Nina Bawden's children's novel is 'The Finding' (1985).
explanation.definitionFit: A discovery is something found, and Bawden's novel about a foundling is titled with that word.

explanation.definitionFit: Hoar-frost is a frozen deposit, and the poem title supplies the source of the quotation at 11.

clue.text: Amis introduced us to one fat one

definitions.text: Amis introduced us to one fat one

parts.words: Amis introduced us to one fat one

explanation.surface: A novelist presented a corpulent character.
explanation.walkthrough: Kingsley Amis's novel 'One Fat Englishman' (1963) follows Roger Micheldene in America.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingsley Amis's novel's title names its portly hero by his nationality, a man from England.
